title: How a Gearbox Really Works (No Grinding) ⚙️
principle: The selected gear spins freely on the output shaft (driven by the layshaft) while the sleeve turns with the shaft on a hub; shifting slides the sleeve, which presses the brass synchronizer ring onto the gear's cone; cone friction brings the gear to shaft speed while the ring (twisted by that friction) blocks the sleeve; once the speeds match the ring turns back in line and the sleeve slides onto the gear's dog teeth, locking gear and shaft together without grinding. Without the ring, the sleeve's teeth meet dog teeth spinning at a different speed and clash (grind).
voiceover: You move the gear lever. What happens inside the gearbox?
This gear spins freely on the shaft, and faster than it.
The sleeve turns with the shaft. The fork slides it.
Without the brass ring, the sleeve hits teeth spinning at a different speed.
So first, the sleeve presses the brass synchro ring onto a cone on the gear.
Friction slows the gear, until both spin at the same speed.
Now the sleeve slides over the dog teeth.
Locked. Now the gear turns the shaft.
The brass ring matches the speeds first. No grind.

firstComment:
Answer: the brass synchro ring 🔧

In a manual gearbox the gears are always in mesh. The gear you want spins freely on the output shaft, at a different speed than the shaft. The sleeve turns with the shaft, and the fork (moved by your gear lever) slides it.

Without a synchro, the sleeve's teeth would hit the gear's dog teeth while they spin at different speeds. They clash: that's the grind.

With a synchro: 1) the sleeve first presses the brass ring onto a cone on the gear. 2) Friction brings the gear to the shaft's speed (here the gear is faster, so it slows down). While the speeds still differ, the ring is twisted slightly and blocks the sleeve. 3) Once the speeds match, the ring turns back in line and the sleeve slides over the dog teeth. 4) Locked: the gear now turns the shaft. No grind.

(Simplified 3D model, slowed down: one gear and one synchro, straight-cut teeth, the clutch is pressed. The "no synchro" part is a what-if. Real gearboxes use helical gears and pointed teeth on the sleeve and ring.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Manual transmission (when the dog clutches are disengaged all gears spin freely around the output shaft; the selector is splined to the shaft and moved by a fork linked to the gear lever; without matched speeds the dog teeth fail to engage and grind; brass synchronizer rings use cone friction to equalize speeds; blocker rings twist slightly from the cone's friction torque and prevent engagement until the speeds are synchronized): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manual_transmission
Lesics, Manual transmission, how it works? (output gears loosely connected to the shaft; hub fixed to the shaft with a sliding sleeve; the sleeve presses the synchronizer ring against the cone, friction makes the gear speed the same as the shaft, then the sleeve slides in and locks the gear): https://lesics.com/manual-transmission-how-it-works.html
altText: 3D animation explaining a manual gearbox synchro, with a voiceover. Inside a car, a hand on the black gear knob moves the lever, under the question How does it shift gears? The console and gearbox case fade away to show a steel shaft, a large gear driven by a smaller gear below, a polished sleeve with a blue fork, and an orange brass ring. Labels name the gear, shaft, sleeve, fork, brass ring, dog teeth and cone. Gear speed and shaft speed bars show the gear spinning faster than the shaft. First, without the brass synchro ring, the sleeve is pushed into the faster dog teeth: they flash red and bounce, and the screen says GRIND. Then with the ring: 1, the brass ring turns see-through and the sleeve presses it onto the gear's cone. 2, with the video slowed down, friction slows the gear until the speed bars turn green, same speed, and two yellow marks line up. 3, the sleeve slides over the dog teeth. 4, locked: gear and shaft spin together and the gear turns the shaft. The payoff text reads Ring matches speeds first. No grind. The case and car fade back in, the hand moves the lever back, and a follow line appears before the video loops.
